new_statements.quote: As a rule, the first syllable of Caac words is stressed, e.g. ‘tabo ‘sit down’, ‘aremaa-n ‘his/her face’ (face-3SG.POSS). New words formed by derivation carry stress on the second syllable, e.g. man-‘tabo ‘chair’ (PLACE-sit.down). Caac syllables typically have the structure V(C) (e.g. o ‘at; to’, âc ‘man’) or CV(C) (e.g. te ‘go down’, pum ‘smoke’).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the word; in words formed by derivation with a prefix (e.g. the place-nominalizer man-), stress stays on the first syllable of the root, i.e. surfaces on the second syllable of the derived word. Root-initial stress; no weight or length sensitivity mentioned.
new_statements.exceptions: Derived words (prefix + root) are stressed on the second syllable, i.e. on the root's first syllable (man-'tabo 'chair'). No other exceptions given.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('Caac words'); cited forms are lexical citation forms including a possessed noun ('aremaa-n). Statement is one sentence in a phonological sketch inside a spatial-semantics thesis; no phonetic or instrumental support.
new_statements.identity_note: Cauchard 2014 describes present-day Caac of the Pouébo (Pweevo) area (villages Saint-Gabriel, Cabwen etc.), i.e. caac1237 proper. Hollyman 1962/1999 call the language 'Caaqac' and distinguish the Pouébo variety from the La Conception (Nouméa) diaspora variety 'Caawac' (no separate glottocode; Glottolog treats both under caac1237).
